beginner.headline: Andrew Bailey: AI Needs Testing, Not Just Rules
beginner.brief: The Bank of England's Governor, Andrew Bailey, spoke about Artificial Intelligence (AI). He said that making rules for AI is not the right first step. Instead, Bailey wants careful testing for AI to find problems. He also said that AI has important risks. But Bailey believes AI should still develop because it has many good benefits. If testing shows problems, it means that testing is necessary.

intermediate.headline: Regulating AI: Prioritizing Rigorous Testing and Safeguards
intermediate.brief: The Governor of the Bank of England has said regulating AI "is not the right place to start." Instead, he called first for rigorous testing to find vulnerabilities and safeguards to contain risk. Andrew Bailey said the risks around AI were real and increasingly significant. Bailey believes AI development should not be halted, as the benefits are immense. However, there must be a system for intervention and to establish boundaries for AI operation. Recently, the debate about AI's potential risks has intensified. Leading AI firm bosses have called for development to slow down and for a co-ordinated approach. President Donald Trump rejected the idea of a slowdown, stating the US leads the AI race. Later, Trump announced executives signed a "morally binding" document for protection from AI's potential risks. Under this agreement, companies are responsible for ensuring the safety of their own technology. In the UK, important work is underway in testing AI, which should help form part of a set of standards. The pace of progress must accelerate, but with a degree of humility, the bank governor added.

advanced.headline: Bailey: Rigorous Testing Must Precede AI Regulation
advanced.brief: Andrew Bailey, Governor of the Bank of England, believes regulating artificial intelligence (AI) "is not the right place to start." Instead, he advocates for "rigorous" testing to find vulnerabilities and establishing safeguards to contain risk. Writing his first article for Substack, Bailey highlighted that the risks associated with AI are "real and increasingly significant." He stated that the development of AI should not be prohibited, "on the contrary, the benefits are immense," but emphasized the need for a system of intervention and clear boundaries. The debate surrounding AI's rapid development and its implications for humanity has recently intensified. Leaders from major AI firms like Anthropic and OpenAI have called for a slowdown and an internationally co-ordinated approach to assessing risks and implementing safeguards. OpenAI specifically chose not to release its latest AI model due to safety concerns. Initially, President Donald Trump rejected the idea of a slowdown, asserting the US lead in the "AI race." However, after a summit with leading AI firms, Trump announced that executives had signed a "morally binding" document to serve as a "form of protection" from potential AI risks. This agreement places responsibility for ensuring the safety of their technology squarely on the companies themselves. In the UK, Bailey noted "important work" underway, including the AI Security Institute, which contributes to forming a set of standards. While acknowledging progress, he stressed that "the pace of progress must accelerate" but also advised proceeding "with a degree of humility." Bailey clarified that failures during testing, where "models will behave unexpectedly," are not evidence of testing failure but rather proof of its necessity. He acknowledged that a more formal regulatory framework might emerge over time, yet maintained that immediate regulation "is not, in my view, the right place to start."
